props.title: Thirst
props.initialSlug: Catholic priest becomes vampire in torrid affair

sections.content: Thirst marks a stunning vampire reimagining from Park Chan-wook, blending Catholic guilt with carnal desire. Like his earlier Oldboy (2003), Park crafts a visceral exploration of moral corruption and redemption. The film follows a priest who becomes a vampire through a medical experiment, setting up a devastating conflict between religious devotion and bloodthirsty urges. It shares DNA with other sophisticated vampire films like Let the Right One In (2008) and Only Lovers Left Alive (2013), but adds distinctly Korean horror elements and Park's signature mix of violence and dark comedy.

sections.content: Park's approach to vampire mythology revolutionizes the genre by grounding supernatural elements in raw human struggle. Like The Hunger (1983) and Near Dark (1987), Thirst treats vampirism as an addiction metaphor, but uniquely frames it through Catholic doctrine about temptation and sin. The film's stunning cinematography by Chung Chung-hoon creates a neo-noir atmosphere that recalls The Addiction (1995), though with a more operatic visual style.

Song Kang-ho's tortured performance as Priest Sang-hyun established a new standard for vampire characterization, influencing later works like Byzantium (2012). The film's exploration of forbidden love echoes Park's other works while adding supernatural stakes. Its unflinching approach to sexuality and violence pushed boundaries in Korean cinema, paving the way for films like The Handmaiden (2016). SUBHEAD: Religious Horror Innovation

movies.title: A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night
movies.slug: Iranian vampire western that similarly reimagines vampire mythology through a cultural lens

sections.content: Park's fusion of Catholic imagery with vampire lore created a unique religious horror hybrid that influenced films like Midnight Mass (2021). The film's meditation on faith and monstrosity shares thematic DNA with The Exorcist (1973) but inverts expectations by making the priest himself the supernatural entity. This approach to religious horror opened new possibilities for the genre, seen in later works like Saint Maud (2019).
